### Home Field widget foundations — neighbour-yielding resize, the widget contract, the action manifest, and Lifecycle1 as the service pattern

`active` · `@legeos.work.home-widget-foundations/2` · part of `@legeos.milestone.m2-session-runs/1`

The Home Field was a dead end for a desktop tester: no way to launch anything, no logout/restart/shutdown, no way to close a window, and a search bar that does nothing outside an expanded drawer. The decision is that every missing capability arrives as a widget on the one screen rather than as a panel or tray, consistent with M2's taskbar-free commitment. This item builds only the foundation those widgets stand on, in four parts. (1) A resize that lets adjacent tiles give up span instead of being evicted: reflow::find_resize, where a yielding neighbour keeps its far edge and the request is clamped to the largest span every neighbour can absorb. (2) The widget contract over TileKind::System, which was a designed-for slot nothing constructed: a descriptor declares what shows at each representation rung and which regions are clickable, and each region names an action rather than coding a behaviour. (3) An action manifest in lege-types, so one declaration drives the shell's labels, the keyboard accelerator and the lege verb. (4) org.legeos.Session.Lifecycle1 on sessiond forwarding to logind, built as the one worked example of the service-interface pattern every future widget follows.

### Either build the AT-SPI bridge and the high-contrast variant, or stop documenting them as shipped

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.accessibility-claimed-but-not-built/1` · part of `@legeos.milestone.m2-session-runs/1`

docs/architecture/accessibility.md states that AT-SPI and Orca ship, and that every shell surface has a high-contrast variant. Neither is true in code. No Cargo.toml in the workspace depends on atspi; no accessible-object tree is registered and no a11y bus is spoken anywhere in shell/lege-shell or crates/. No high-contrast token, theme or setting exists in the shell. distro/seeds/a11y.seed really does install orca, at-spi2-core and speech-dispatcher — which is what makes this worse than a plain omission: a blind user can install LegeOS, start Orca, and meet a desktop that says nothing, because the shell paints itself with a custom rasterizer and exposes no name, role or state for any tile, drawer row or widget region. A toolkit would have carried the bridge; painting everything means owning it.

What is real: the focus ring is a genuine distinct indicator, reduced motion is a respected setting, and the field is deliberately keyboard-complete with pointer parity enforced by a gate. Those are the foundations; they are not a screen reader.

Two defensible outcomes and one indefensible one. Build the bridge; or correct the documentation and the seed to say plainly that assistive-technology support is not yet implemented. What must not persist is the current state, where the docs assert a capability a user could depend on and be stranded by. Correcting the documentation costs almost nothing and should not wait for the implementation — that part is separable and worth doing first, whatever is decided about the rest.

### Home Field widgets — every missing desktop capability as a tile on the one screen

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1` · part of `@legeos.milestone.m2-session-runs/1`

A gap review of the Home Field against what any desktop of the last twenty years offers found that a cold session gives the user eight drawer tiles and the message "open an application and it will appear", with no way to open one. Application tiles are derived only from windows that are already running and are removed when the last one closes, so the launcher route is circular. There is no logout, restart, shutdown, suspend or lock; no way to close a window; no volume, brightness or battery; no notification rendering despite sessiond hosting the notification server; no context menus; and the field's own search bar does nothing outside an expanded drawer. The decision is that each of these arrives as a widget on the single screen — information first, sub-clickable, opening a window only as a deliberate second step — rather than as a panel, a dock or a tray, which is consistent with M2's taskbar-free commitment and with homefield.md's rule that the launcher is inventory and the home screen is working memory. @legeos.work.home-widget-foundations built the framework; this item is the umbrella for the widgets themselves and for the window controls that are still missing.

### Files.Trash1 — see what is in the trash, put an item back, and empty it

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.trash-that-can-be-seen-and-emptied/1` · part of `@legeos.milestone.m2-session-runs/1`

The trash cannot be looked at. trash::list is implemented and freedesktop-correct — it parses .trashinfo, handles the per-volume .Trash-$uid, sorts newest first (services/lege-filed/src/trash.rs:198) — and is called from exactly one place in the repository: a test. No D-Bus interface exposes it, so the shell's Trash drawer renders the operations journal filtered to trash and restore, and says so honestly in its own empty state; its header comment names Files.Trash1 as the interface it wants (shell/lege-shell/src/drawers/trash.rs:1-15). There is no empty-trash anywhere — no method, no verb, no control — and no explicit restore action in the Files app, which has Trash and Undo but no Restore. Permanent delete is modelled and executable and no UI ever constructs it.

Design settled by the audit. Trash1 gets one read method, List, which is the thing Operations1 genuinely cannot answer and which must sweep every trash this user has — the home trash and each mounted volume's — not just the one. Restore, DeletePermanently and Empty are thin validating wrappers over the same FileService::start that Operations1.Start uses, so a large empty keeps its progress, its journal and its crash-resume, and a restore keeps its undo, instead of growing a second execution path with a different story. Empty sweeps server-side rather than making a client list-then-delete, which would race. A Changed signal, emitted from the single place operations complete, keeps the drawer and the Files app live whichever client did the mutating.

Order: interface, service and proxy together (check-interfaces and check-proxies only go green as a set), then the CLI verbs, then the shell drawer's real listing, then the Files app's trash place last — that one is the largest piece, because it means teaching a directory browser to render a listing that is not a directory, with different columns, different actions and a confirmation rule of its own. The Files app is the cut line if budget runs short; the CLI gives a working path meanwhile.

The undo defect this area also carried is already fixed at git:464e069b7b2769bc5e0ab34e8191b65f9101e7db and is not part of this item.

### Next Home usability sequence — adaptable Home, complete folder surfaces, then common Settings

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.home-surface-usability-next/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-field/1`

Carry the Home surface from a fixed demonstration layout to an ordinary daily desktop in the order set by the user on 2026-08-31.

First, make Home itself adaptable: configurable Home-only panels/rails/docks, automatic panel layouts for different output shapes, user-invoked arrangements for all open windows, and immediate reversible switching among those arrangements. Preserve truly chrome-free fullscreen application work and refine bare Super from release-only toggling into immediate press/hold Home reveal with shortcut-safe semantics.

Second, make folders and composite shortcut panes the Home file objects. Build copy/cut/paste, drag and drop, delete/trash and the remaining ordinary file verbs on the multi-selection foundation; then add deterministic sorting and list-versus-thumbnail presentation. Loose individual file tiles are explicitly not part of this model.

Third, make the graphical Settings app adjust the common controls a person expects: resolution/refresh/rotation/scale, mouse and trackpad behaviour, and appearance/theme/material choices. Accessibility remains deferred behind these product-completeness items per the user's standing priority.

### Copy, cut, paste, drag/drop, trash and ordinary file actions inside Home folder surfaces

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.file-operations-from-home/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-surface-usability-next/1`

Complete ordinary file manipulation inside expanded Home folders and shortcut panes, using the multi-selection model that now exists. Ctrl+C/Ctrl+X/Ctrl+V copy or move every selected item through Files.Operations1; the clipboard advertises and accepts standard URI-list data where possible so Files and other desktop applications interoperate. Delete moves real files to Trash through the journalled service and reports an undo route. Rename, New Folder, Properties and Copy Path remain part of the same coherent action surface.

Implement drag and drop with typed destinations. Dropping onto a real folder copies or moves according to the declared gesture/modifier; dropping onto a shortcut pane adds references unless the user explicitly chooses a file operation; dropping onto an application resolves an Open With/application action; dragging out exports URI-list data. Bare Home never accepts an individual file as a loose tile and instead routes it to a shortcut pane per the governing object model.

All bulk operations are one journalled operation with one progress/error surface and one undo. The Home field-layout undo and file-operation undo remain distinct internally, but the focused surface routes Ctrl+Z to the most recent applicable action and says which action will be undone. Conflict, permission, partial-failure and cross-device cases are answered by the file service rather than guessed by the shell.

### One-press reversible arrangements for all open windows

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.reversible-window-arrangement-presets/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-surface-usability-next/1`

Add a Home control made of manifest-declared buttons that arranges the eligible open windows on an output into useful shapes: one-window focus/full-output, halves, thirds, quarters/grid, a large-focus-plus-side-stack layout, and a cushion/treemap-style packing inspired by Silvaview. The compositor owns window geometry and recoverability; the shell only requests a named preset and renders its preview/button.

The first preset request snapshots every affected window's prior geometry and state. Choosing a different preset recomputes directly from that baseline and the current eligible window set, so a person can audition arrangements by pressing buttons without walking an undo history. Restore returns surviving windows exactly to the saved baseline, repaired only when output topology makes an old rectangle unreachable. Closed windows disappear cleanly; newly opened windows join on the next explicit preset press rather than causing surprise background retiling. The feature is user-invoked arrangement, not a permanently enforced tiling window manager.

Arrangement controls live on Home. An application can still be fullscreen with no Home chrome visible, and the compositor's shell-independent recovery routes remain available.

## [Home Field widgets — every missing desktop capability as a tile on the one screen](ACTIVE-WORK.md#home-field-widgets--every-missing-desktop-capability-as-a-tile-on-the-one-screen) `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

### Launcher widget — make a cold session able to open its first application

`active` · `@legeos.work.home-widget-launcher/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

A launcher widget that lists installed applications, filters as the user types, and launches through Launcher1. This is the single most load-bearing gap: without it a freshly booted session cannot open anything at all, because application tiles are derived from windows that already exist (field_model::merge_apps) and are removed when the last one closes. The inventory is already in the shell — AppIdentity1.ListApps is fetched every three seconds into ShellApp::apps and its only consumer today is a grep for nm-tray — and Launcher1.Launch already works and is already called for the network control and for opening files. The widget itself is small; the prerequisites below are not.

### Window close and resize, and a pointer path for every action that today has only a chord

`active` · `@legeos.work.window-controls-and-mouse-parity/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

Give the user a way to close and resize a window, and give every declared action a mouse route. `window.close` is declared in the action manifest and reachable from nothing: lege_shell_toplevel_v1.close exists in the protocol and ShellBridge::close exists in the shell with zero callers, so a window with no client-side decorations — most XWayland clients, xterm, SDL applications — cannot be closed by the user at all. Interactive resize is a deliberate no-op in xdg_shell.rs::resize_request, and decoration mode is forced to ClientSide unconditionally, so such a window can never be resized either. Separately, thirteen declared actions are reachable only by keyboard; the action manifest's own rule is that a chord is an accelerator recorded alongside a menu entry and never the only route to a capability, so those need a pointer or menu path.

### Notification widget — the tile and the read-back path shipped; per-notification dismiss, actions and any push remain

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.home-widget-notifications/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

Superseded in part by what shipped on 2026-08-30. Revision 1's premise — that the shell contains no notification rendering whatsoever, and that sessiond offers no read-back — no longer holds. org.legeos.Notifications1 serves ListActive, Dismiss, ClearAll and a Changed signal alongside the full org.freedesktop.Notifications implementation, and the shell has a notifications system widget (shell/lege-shell/src/surface/widgets/mod.rs:144) showing a headline count and up to three app — summary lines, with a clear-all region wired to ClearAll.

What remains is most of what makes notifications useful. There is no per-notification dismiss, only bulk clear. A notification's actions cannot be invoked from the shell — ActionInvoked is served but never emitted by any surface — so a notification offering Reply or Open is decorative. Nothing is pushed: no toast, no OSD, nothing appears unprompted, so a notification is seen only if the user happens to look at the tile, which for a message or a finished job is close to not being notified at all. The three-line cap does not grow with the tile.

History is readable through Settings — History or lege settings --page history, so nothing is lost; it is just not surfaced where a user would look.

### Volume, brightness and battery widgets, and the services they need — none of which exist yet

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.home-widget-status-instruments/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

Volume, brightness and battery as widgets, each backed by a service interface following the Lifecycle1 pattern. All three are absent from the whole repository, not merely from the shell: there is no audio client of any kind (no PipeWire, PulseAudio or ALSA code — the only mentions are cgroup protections naming the pipewire and wireplumber units so the resource governor never kills them), no backlight code, and no battery reading. crates/lege-hwdetect is GPU detection only. So each of these is a service to write first and a widget second, which is the order services-not-indicators requires anyway.

### Drive the compositor's ext-session-lock-v1 so Lifecycle1.Lock stops returning NotSupported

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.session-lock-client/1` · part of `@legeos.work.home-widgets/1`

Make locking the session actually lock it. The compositor implements ext-session-lock-v1 in full (compositor/lege-comp/src/session_lock.rs) and ADR-0010 makes the lock screen compositor-owned, "one provider by construction". What has never existed is anything that drives it: no client calls lock(), so there is no lock surface and no lock. Lifecycle1.Lock is declared with the interface shape settled and returns NotSupported rather than reporting a success it did not achieve. Making it real means giving lege-sessiond a Wayland lock-manager client, which is a substantial piece of work and was scoped out of the foundations deliberately rather than overlooked.

## Unparented

### Declare every user-facing action once, and generate the menu, the cheat sheet and the CLI verb from it

`proposed` · `@legeos.work.action-manifest-one-declaration-three-surfaces/1`

LegeOS already commits to every capability being reachable from the CLI, the portal, the shell and Settings (M1 evidence m1-clients-reachable; docs/architecture/accessibility.md: "everything the shell shows is available through lege too"). Today that is a discipline maintained by hand across four implementations, and nothing prevents them drifting. Omarchy demonstrates the mechanism that makes it structural: one declaration — `o.bind(chord, human_label, action)` — is simultaneously the keybinding, the row in a mouse-navigable menu tree, and the entry in a cheat sheet generated from the same table, so the documentation cannot fall out of date with the behaviour because it is not a separate artefact. Adopt the pattern: an action manifest (id, human label, optional chord, CLI verb, availability predicate) living in a service crate rather than the shell, with the shell's menu, the discoverability surface and `lege`'s subcommand table all rendered from it. The manifest belonging to a service rather than the shell is what keeps it consistent with services-not-indicators: the shell renders the manifest, it does not own it.
